themes.label: Motivation for range-based volatility estimation
themes.need: A researcher choosing an estimation method for stochastic volatility models needs to understand why traditional Gaussian QMLE, GMM, and likelihood-based approaches are inefficient or impractical, motivating the range as an alternative volatility proxy.
themes.distributed_justification: The author-affiliation footnote (lines 13-14) interrupts the continuous argument for why traditional SV estimators are inadequate and why the range is proposed as a remedy.

themes.label: Continuous-time SV model and discretization
themes.need: Someone building or implementing a stochastic volatility model needs the general continuous-time diffusion formulation and its piecewise-constant discretization into a Gaussian AR(1) log-volatility process.

themes.label: State-space representation and Gaussian QMLE
themes.need: Someone estimating a discretized stochastic volatility model needs the linear state-space transition/measurement equations and the Gaussian quasi-maximum-likelihood procedure via the Kalman filter, including its consistency/inefficiency tradeoffs.

themes.label: Distributional properties of absolute/squared return proxies
themes.need: Someone assessing why log absolute or squared returns are inefficient volatility proxies needs their theoretical distribution (heavy skew and kurtosis) and empirical confirmation via Table I and Figure 1a.

themes.label: Log range proxy: efficiency, near-normality, and history
themes.need: Someone deciding whether to use the price range as a volatility proxy needs its formal definition, the theoretical derivation of its superior efficiency and near-Gaussian distribution, and its estimation history since Parkinson (1980).

themes.label: Robustness of range vs realized volatility to microstructure noise
themes.need: Someone choosing between range-based and realized-volatility estimators under market microstructure noise (bid-ask bounce) needs the theoretical argument plus a systematic Monte Carlo comparison of their bias and RMSE across sampling frequencies.
themes.distributed_justification: Section II.F poses the robustness-to-microstructure-noise question with a theoretical argument and single-day illustration; Section III.C, page-distant, is the systematic repeated-sample Monte Carlo confirmation of that same need (intro-poses/later-resolves pattern). Remaining span breaks are forced by interposed Figure 4/5 caption-stub trash.

themes.label: Monte Carlo simulation design (DGP and parameters)
themes.need: Someone replicating the paper's Monte Carlo study needs the data-generating process (Euler discretization), sample-size grid, and calibrated parameter values used to simulate SV price paths.

themes.label: MC parameter-estimation accuracy: range vs return-based QMLE vs exact ML
themes.need: Someone deciding whether range-based Gaussian QMLE reliably estimates SV model parameters needs the Monte Carlo bias/RMSE comparison against absolute-return QMLE and exact ML, including sensitivity to trading frequency and sample size.
themes.distributed_justification: Figure 3's image placeholder (raw plot content, trash lines 408-416) splits the continuous parameter-estimate discussion; both spans describe the same T=1000/T=500 estimation-accuracy results (Tables II-III, Figure 3).

themes.label: MC latent-volatility extraction accuracy
themes.need: Someone wants to know how accurately range-based versus absolute-return-based QMLE recovers the latent volatility path itself, not just parameters, via the Kalman-filter extraction error statistics.

themes.label: Exchange-rate data: futures vs spot justification
themes.need: Someone constructing range-based volatility measures from currency data needs justification for using futures rather than spot prices and a description of the IMM futures dataset (1978-1998, five currencies).

themes.label: Table V: volatility-proxy distributions and persistence across currencies
themes.need: Someone wants empirical evidence that the log range dominates log absolute returns in efficiency and reveals stronger volatility persistence across five major exchange rates, via unconditional moments and autocorrelations.
themes.distributed_justification: The Section IV.B heading and its continuing sentence (theme t12) interrupt the Table V introduction and the table itself.

themes.label: One-factor SV model: range-based estimates reveal misspecification
themes.need: Someone fitting a one-factor SV model to exchange-rate data needs to see how range-based estimates and residual diagnostics expose serious one-factor misspecification, in contrast to absolute-return-based estimates that appear adequate.
themes.distributed_justification: The section heading's sentence is cut mid-word by the interposed Table V content (theme t11) and resumes at line 544.

themes.label: Two-factor SV model estimation and residual diagnostics
themes.need: Someone needs the two-factor SV model specification (persistent + transient components) and its range-based estimates and residual diagnostics confirming the two-factor model is adequate where the one-factor model was not.

themes.label: Empirical verification of log-range residual normality
themes.need: Someone wants to confirm empirically that the two-factor model's measurement-equation residuals under the log-range proxy are indistinguishable from Gaussian, verifying the paper's theoretical normality claim, via residual moments and QQ plots.
themes.distributed_justification: A caption-stub trash span (680-696, raw histogram/QQ-plot images) separates the normality-verification prose from its own Figure 6 caption.

themes.label: Why range-based analysis reveals two volatility factors
themes.need: Someone wants the conceptual explanation for why range-based estimation, unlike absolute-return-based estimation, clearly reveals the need for two volatility factors, tied to the range's superior information about the volatility of volatility.

themes.label: Structural two-factor models vs reduced-form long-memory models
themes.need: Someone comparing structural multi-factor SV models to fractionally-integrated long-memory reduced-form models needs the argument for why the structural two-factor decomposition is more interpretable and may forecast volatility better.

themes.label: Future directions: multivariate range extensions and comparison to realized volatility
themes.need: Someone extending the range-based estimation framework needs pointers toward multivariate extensions of range-based volatility proxies and a deeper open comparison between range-based and realized-volatility estimators.

unassigned.reason: Pure recap/literature-context paragraph restating the already-covered two-factor consensus finding (t13/t15); no standalone answerable practitioner need beyond what those themes already cover.
